lessons.title: Seed cane and preparing to plant
lessons.html:
Seed cane and preparing to plant

Sugarcane is not grown from seed like mealies. It is planted from pieces of stalk called setts (seed cane). Each sett has buds at the nodes (the joints). A new shoot grows from each bud, and roots grow from the node.

Good seed cane

  • Comes from a healthy, approved seed cane field, ideally certified free of diseases such as smut and ratoon stunting disease.
  • Is young and fresh, with healthy, swollen buds.
  • Is the variety (cultivar) the farm manager has chosen for that field.
  • Is planted as soon as possible after cutting, so the buds do not dry out.

Preparing the setts

  1. Remove the dry leaves carefully so you do not damage the buds.
  2. Cut the stalks into setts with a sharp, clean knife. Your supervisor will tell you how many buds each sett must have.
  3. Cut cleanly. Do not crush the stalk.
  4. Throw out setts with dead, damaged or missing buds, or with red rot inside.
  5. If the farm treats setts (for example with hot water or a fungicide), this is done by trained workers following the label or the farm's instructions.

The planting furrow

The land is usually ploughed and furrows are opened with a tractor before planting. The furrows should be straight, at the right spacing and the right depth. Fertiliser may be placed in the furrow before planting, as the manager instructs.

Safety

  • Wear gloves, boots and long sleeves. Cane leaves cut skin.
  • Carry the cane knife with the blade down.
  • If setts were treated with chemicals, wear the PPE the label requires and wash your hands before eating.
  • Lift bundles of seed cane with bent knees and get help with heavy loads.

lessons.title: Planting and covering the setts
lessons.html:
Planting and covering the setts

Laying the setts

  1. Walk along the furrow carrying setts in a bag or bundle.
  2. Lay the setts flat in the bottom of the furrow, end to end. Some farms ask for a slight overlap or a double row. Follow the farm's planting rule so there are no gaps.
  3. Lay the setts so the buds face to the sides, not straight up or down. This helps shoots come up evenly.
  4. Press the setts into moist soil so they have good contact with the soil.

Covering

  • Cover the setts with a thin, even layer of soil using a hoe or by foot, to the depth your supervisor gives.
  • Too deep: shoots take long to come up and some may die.
  • Too shallow: setts dry out in the sun.
  • Firm the soil lightly so there are no air pockets.

Planting at the right time

Plant when the soil is moist, or irrigate soon after planting. Setts dry out quickly in hot, dry soil.

After planting

  • Check the field after a few weeks. Look for gaps where shoots have not come up.
  • Fill gaps (gap filling) with new setts or seedlings as instructed.
  • Keep the young cane free of weeds; weeds compete strongly with young cane.

Recording

Write down the field number, date, variety, number of bundles planted and any problems such as dry soil. This helps the farm plan and trace any disease.

Common mistakes

MistakeResult
Gaps between settsEmpty patches and less cane
Planting old, dry seed canePoor germination
Covering too deepSlow or failed shoots
Using diseased caneDisease spreads to the new field

Key points

  • Sugarcane is planted from setts with healthy buds.
  • Use fresh, healthy seed cane of the right variety from an approved source.
  • Lay setts end to end with no gaps, buds facing the sides.
  • Cover to the right depth and firm the soil.
  • Check for gaps later and keep the young cane free of weeds.
